issues.description: The template repository provides an Order class (Order.java) but the problem statement and the solution expect a Meal class. In the template, Meal.java is empty, while Order.java defines the meal-like structure. This class-name/type mismatch will confuse students: the exercise and UML refer to Meal, constructors and method signatures (e.g., SealSaloon.calculateTotalPrice(Meal)) expect a Meal type, but the starter code exposes an Order type instead, preventing straightforward implementation and compilation until students rename or duplicate the class.
issues.suggestedFix: Update the template repository to include a Meal class matching the specification (constructor Meal(String, String[]) and corresponding getters). Either rename Order.java to Meal.java or add a Meal.java that mirrors the structure in Order.java, and remove or clarify the presence of Order.java so students implement against the Meal type described in the problem statement.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution refer to a conceptual entity named 'Meal', but the template repository provides an implemented class named 'Order' (and an empty Meal.java). This mismatch (Meal vs Order) creates a mapping barrier: students reading the problem expect to find/implement a Meal class and related API, but the template offers Order, causing confusion about which class to use or modify.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the naming consistent across artifacts by providing a Meal class in the template (or renaming the implemented Order class to Meal) with the same API as shown in the solution (getName(), getIngredients()). Remove or deprecate the extra Order class so students clearly map the problem description to the template code.
